articles.title: Japan extends transition bond push despite fossil-fuel reliance
articles.summary: Japanese government bonds have rallied alongside other so-called safe-haven assets in recent weeks as technology-sector jitters unsettled investors.
articles.preview: Japan sold its fifth climate transition bond of the year, remaining the only government to use the designation despite the country’s increasing reliance on fossil fuels since the start of the war in Iran. The ¥250 billion ($1.6 billion) issuance attracted steady demand with a bid-to-cover ratio of 3.84, compared with 4.62 in May, and an average of 3.79 since issuance began in February 2024. The highest yield accepted was 2.2%. The sale comes against a strengthening backdrop for the broader domestic bond market.
articles.body:
Japan sold its fifth climate transition bond of the year, remaining the only government to use the designation despite the country’s increasing reliance on fossil fuels since the start of the war in Iran.

The ¥250 billion ($1.6 billion) issuance attracted steady demand with a bid-to-cover ratio of 3.84, compared with 4.62 in May, and an average of 3.79 since issuance began in February 2024. The highest yield accepted was 2.2%.

The sale comes against a strengthening backdrop for the broader domestic bond market.

Japanese government bonds have rallied alongside other so-called safe-haven assets in recent weeks as technology-sector jitters unsettled investors.

That marks a reversal from earlier this year, when concerns about the nation’s fiscal spending and inflation, coupled with a global bond selloff, sent yields to multi-decade highs.

The latest issuance of transition bonds is the 11th by the Japanese government, part of a ¥150 trillion program through 2033 to channel capital to specific emissions reduction programs.

Issuers in the country remain the dominant force behind climate-transition bonds, accounting for about 90% of the market since 2024, according to data

The Japanese government has issued more than $30 billion of the debt so far, most of it purchased by the Bank of Japan and other local institutional investors. South Korean and Chinese entities are among other issuers that have sold transition bonds.

Environmental think-tanks have criticized Japan for reinforcing its reliance on fossil-fuel imports despite a goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 60% by fiscal 2035 from 2013 levels.

With the Iran war threatening supplies, the government has doubled down on oil, releasing strategic reserves and creating a new plan aimed at diversifying sources away from the Middle East while also investing in new supply.

The country remains the world’s fifth-largest carbon dioxide emitter, with coal, oil and gas accounting for more than 80% of its energy supply last year, according to the International Energy Agency.

Proceeds from this fiscal year’s transition bond sales are earmarked for eligible projects in artificial intelligence, semiconductors, robotics and nuclear technologies such as fusion energy, according to Japan Credit Rating Agency.

Only 4% will go toward making renewable energy “a major power source,” including efforts to build supply chains and promote the use of perovskite solar cells.

articles.body:
The UK government’s decision to impose a ban on trade in goods from illegal settlements was not decisive in how Israelis voted in their general election, but a majority think the Israeli government’s settlements policy should change if it is going to lead to further sanctions, a new poll of Israelis shows.

There had been fierce criticism of the UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s decision in September to impose a trade ban and wider sanctions on illegal settlements, with some claiming it would drive Israeli voters into the arms of Benjamin Netanyahu.

A survey last month by Israeli social research group aChord shows overall support for foreign sanctions on violent settlers in the West Bank, but there was little support for the UK’s ban on trade with goods from illegal settlements, with many fearing it would end up being extended across Israel.

The survey is unique in showing how much the tougher line on Israel adopted by Britain and some foreign states was affecting the thinking of Israeli voters, and the extent to which Israelis thought it was a response to Israel’s actions or born of hostility to Israel, or even antisemitism.

The survey showed that three-quarters of supporters of the bloc backing Netanyahu said UK sanctions and trade ban policies towards Israel did not affect their vote at all, and to the small extent that they changed anyone’s vote, they shifted voters both ways, leaving no detectable net effect.

Just over three-quarters of all those surveyed (76) – had heard of the UK government announcement on settlements, even if 18 % had only heard the broad headline. Four-fifths of those that were aware of the announcement knew that the policy applied to the West Bank, and not the whole of Israel.

Israel’s relations with the west were “important or very important” to 60% of the supporters of the Change bloc of parties backing Gadi Eisenkot in deciding their vote. But even then these relationships came fifth in importance in a proffered group of six motives for voting. Only 30% of supporters of the Netanyahu bloc said relations with the west mattered in the same way.

But 71% of voters for the opposition Change bloc said the Israeli government should adapt its settlements policy to avoid an escalation of sanctions. Only 14% of Netanyahu bloc voters agreed, most saying instead that the government should continue the policy “whatever the price”.

A plurality of the public – 50% – said the settlement and construction policy in the West Bank should be adjusted to avoid sanctions escalation and international isolation, with 71% of Eisenkot bloc supporters agreeing to this proposition. Support for a change in the policy is strongest among supporters of the Arab parties.

The finding prompted Hannah Weisfeld, the director of the British-Jewish organisation Yachad, to claim the research “illustrates that the Israeli public certainly recognises that if there is not a policy shift in relation to settlement enterprise, the international community is likely to try to create an incentive to shift things from the outside. If anything, that highlights the importance of UK and other allies taking action that targets the occupation.”

The survey also showed that concerns about foreign sanctions are highest when voters feel they will suffer a high personal price. Only 36% of all those surveyed agreed that the settlement policy should continue even if sanctions on banks that finance construction in illegal settlements led either to higher interest rates, difficulties in transferring money abroad, or using credit cards abroad. The poll suggests that the more people feel they will be damaged personally, the more they oppose the settlement policy.

A majority of all Israelis surveyed (52%) support sanctions on individual violent settlers, so long as the sanctions are imposed only on those acting violently, but 70% of Netanyahu bloc supporters oppose foreign sanctions in all circumstances.

There is much less widespread support for the policy of banning the import of goods from the illegal settlement, with 63% of all those surveyed opposing the ban and 26% either supporting the measure outright, or saying they would if it were underlined that the ban would not apply to goods from outside settlements.

articles.title: South Korea’s president vows to make bold AI investment in record budget push
articles.summary: South Korea’s economy has been heavily boosted by demand for advanced chips used in AI, lifting exports and the earnings of memory chip makers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.
articles.preview: South Korea’s economy has been heavily boosted by demand for advanced chips used in AI, lifting exports and the earnings of memory chip makers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. SEOUL: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung vowed on Monday (Nov 2) to make bold investments in artificial intelligence to boost the country's economic growth potential, in an address to parliament seeking approval for next year's budget.
articles.body:
South Korea’s economy has been heavily boosted by demand for advanced chips used in AI, lifting exports and the earnings of memory chip makers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

SEOUL: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung vowed on Monday (Nov 2) to make bold investments in artificial intelligence to boost the country's economic growth potential, in an address to parliament seeking approval for next year's budget.

"We will invest 21.3 trillion won (US$15.97 billion), nearly twice this year’s amount, in AI and the three megaprojects of semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centres," Lee said.

His administration proposed in September increasing government spending by a record 12.8 per cent next year to 820.9 trillion won aiming to strengthen South Korea’s technological edge as global competition over AI intensifies.

South Korea’s economy has been heavily boosted by demand for advanced chips used in AI, lifting exports and the earnings of memory chip makers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

Asia's fourth-largest economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter on chip exports and investment. From January to October, exports totalled US$930 billion, on track to exceed US$1 trillion this year and make South Korea the fourth country in the world to reach the milestone after the United States, China and Germany.

Lee said annual exports of US$1 trillion were now within reach, but warned that the benefits were not being shared evenly.

"We must make a great transition from ‘growth for the few,’ in which opportunities and gains are concentrated among certain regions, classes and a small number of companies, to ‘growth for all,’” he said.

The budget includes a 162.3 trillion won Future Response Fund, financed largely by additional tax revenue from the semiconductor boom, to support growth industries, young people, regional development and education while providing a buffer against future revenue shortfalls.

Lee is simultaneously pursuing nationwide megaprojects centred on chips, physical AI and data centres, including an 800 trillion won private sector chip buildout led by Samsung and SK Hynix in the country's southwest.

articles.preview: Supermarkets across Europe have experienced temperature-control meddling The fake nuclear threats to Ukraine came as Russia resumed its attacks on the southern city of Kherson , just hours after the end of a ceasefire during which hundreds of people were evacuated from the nearby Kremlin-controlled town of Oleshky. Kherson’s military administration said a Russian drone hit a hospital at 7.40am. Video footage showed wrecked rooms, with windows blown out, doors broken, and debris on the street. Nobody was hurt, officials said. Continue reading...
articles.body:
Supermarket chain Coop confirms it uses same system as French supermarkets hacked last month

The information we’re getting about how the cyber-attack occurred is still piecemeal; but we’re getting more details from from different affected supermarket chains.

In Sweden, the Coop supermarket chain just released a statement confirming a cyber incident involving “unauthorised tampering” in their fridge’s cooling systems.

Noticeably, Coop also confirmed that one of their system suppliers is Danfoss, the same Danish company which supplied temperature controllers to the French supermarkets attacked last month.

In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers that were mostly supplied by Danfoss. They disabled the alarm systems before adjusting the thermostats or extending the defrost programme by hours.

Several of the affected supermarket chains today say that fridge and freezer temperatures were pushed to 50C. From the incident in Estonia, we know too that the computer programme controlling the temperature controls was hacked into, according to authorities there.

Governments have been warning citizens to prepare food and water stockpiles

Given the geographic scale of this latest wave of fridge cyber-attacks – with stores in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Estonia and Ireland all affected- it’s worth remembering the recent warnings from governments urging citizens to prepare food and water stockpiles.

Just a fortnight ago, the UK government blasted out its ‘Be Ready’ campaign, urging households to be prepared with three days’ worth of food and water (about nine litres per person) at home, in case of emergencies.

Fridge hacking wasn’t put down as a reason – the first known incidents of this type on this scale, were only reported in France in October. But there has been growing official concerns about the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.

The EU food commissioner has said that the bloc’s food security isn’t in question, but these latest fridge attacks will be another wake-up call for citizens.

EU food commissioner says fridge hacks aimed at 'disrupting food supply'

This latest wave of cyberattacks targeting supermarkets across Europe is “a deliberate attempt to disrupt” the EU’s food supply, says Christophe Hansen, the European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food.

He added it was also aimed at undermining the public’s confidence, and while “food security is not currently at risk, ... the food waste and impact on businesses are real.”

Reuters has a quick snap that an EU spokesperson has said it will continue to work with member states over the fridge and freezer cyber-attacks reported earlier.

The spokesperson insisted the EU had several tools in place to deal with such incidents, but that it showed that cyber-attacks can disrupt the daily lives of citizens.

Three men accused of causing a deadly explosion in the heart of Athens’ tourist district by allegedly stealing copper piping from the local gas supply network were appearing in court Monday for a preliminary hearing, AP reports.

The September blast killed six people when it caused the collapse of a two-story residential building in the Greek capital’s historic Plaka district, near the ancient Acropolis. The three suspects allegedly removed piping from the building’s gas supply network to sell the copper as scrap, and face charges including arson, manslaughter with possible intent, causing a deadly explosion and causing dangerous bodily harm.

Back to the political crisis in Belgium for a moment where earlier this morning prime minister Bart De Wever tendered his resignation to King Philippe. A statement said Philippe was “withholding his decision” for now.

The Brussels Times reports that “De Wever will visit Philippe again on Friday, when the king will make a final decision on his resignation.”

De Wever’s move came after the five-party coalition he leads could not agree on a budget. If his resignation is accepted, then either another party might be invited to attempt to form a coalition based on the existing parliamentary balance, or new elections may be held.

Irish and Estonian supermarkets also targeted in freezer cyber-hacks

SuperValu, Ireland’s third-largest supermarket chain, says it’s also had some of its freezer temperatures in-store tampered with, in this second wave of suspected cyber hackings of supermarkets across Europe.

SuperValu said a cyber incident had taken place at 13 of its 233 stores – and that it’s also been forced to throw out chilled and frozen products that have spoiled.

In Estonia, a manufacturer of the affected fridge technology said one its clients had been affected, and the cyber-hackers had gotten into a computer controlling the refrigeration levels and turned the temperature up to 50C. The Selver chain said one of its stores was affected.

As we’ve been reporting, supermarkets across Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg all experienced this temperature- control meddling overnight.

In Belgium, affected chains include Spar, Carrefour, Delhaize, Intermarche, and in Sweden, ICA, Coop and Axfood.

Carrefour said 15 of its stores in Belgium had been affected by the hack. The chain was targeted in a mass cyber attack in France last month.

“It’s a cyberattack, there is no other reason,” Carrefour Belgium spokesman Mich Vergauwen told AFP news agency, but noting the “impact is very limited”.

He said 15 stores among 700 in total were affected but not every refrigerator was impacted.

Russia resumes attacks, with fortified positions, after Oleshky ceasefire

Luke Harding

The fake nuclear threats to Ukraine came as Russia resumed its attacks on the southern city of Kherson, just hours after the end of a ceasefire during which hundreds of people were evacuated from the nearby Kremlin-controlled town of Oleshky.

Kherson’s military administration said a Russian drone hit a hospital at 7.40am. Video footage showed wrecked rooms, with windows blown out, doors broken, and debris on the street. Nobody was hurt, officials said.

There is evidence that the Russian army used the six-day ceasefire to strengthen its positions in Oleskhy and to rotate in new troops. Bodies of dead civilians were also removed from a hospital morgue.

Footage shared with Sky News showed Russian soldiers deploying heavy military equipment and delivering ammunition. They carried large bags into burned out houses and buildings and disappeared into basements, the broadcaster reported.

Armoured vehicles were spotted moving around Oleshky’s streets. The occupied city is 3 miles from Kherson, on the opposite bank of the Dnipro River. Before last week’s truce, resupply was difficult because of the threat from Ukrainian kamikaze drones.

According to the commander of Ukraine’s 34th Separate Marine Brigade, Dmitry Pulinets, Russian soldiers were previously unable to drive in the city, “neither during the day, nor at night, nor in bad weather”.

“Now they have this opportunity. And for the last few days this movement has been happening constantly,” he told Sky News.

The ceasefire expired at 11pm on Sunday. Both sides hailed the local pause in the fighting – the most significant since 2022 – as a success. Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who visited Oleshky to coordinate the mission, said it could be repeated on other parts of the frontline.

However, Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Monday there were no plans for another truce elsewhere. He said it was “standard practice” for army units to regroup in “such circumstances” and added that he assumed Ukraine’s armed forces had “done the same”.

'I was briefly terrified'- Kyiv residents on fake nuclear warning

Luke Harding

My colleague, Luke Harding in Kyiv, has also filed this dispatch from the Ukrainian capital where residents received those fake alerts last night, saying they were at risk of an imminent nuclear strike.

Many residents ignored the alerts, which began shortly before 11pm local time, assuming that the app had been compromised.

Others were scared. “I was briefly terrified,” one woman, Nina, said. “I lay on my bed and wondered what was coming.”

The app reported a high possibility of nuclear radiation late on Sunday. It also wrongly warned of a chemical threat to the Ukrainian capital and street-to-street fighting. The messages were written in English with spelling mistakes, as well as in Ukrainian.

A message written in Russian also claimed Ukraine was about to be hit by Oreshnik missiles, which can carry nuclear warheads. The Kremlin has used the ballistic weapon three times before, hitting the Kyiv region, and the cities of Dnipro and Lviv.

It was unclear on Monday who might have carried out the cyber-raid, or why. Russian officials claimed hackers had also sent fake emergency alerts there after gaining access to the app of the ministry for emergencies, based in Moscow.

One of their posts mentioned the hacking group Hitcore. Mash, a Russian Telegram channel with links to the security services, said it had spoken to representatives of Hitcore and that they had claimed responsibility for the attack. The report could not be verified.

My colleague, Jon Henley, is covering this latest wave of supermarket fridge cyber-attacks.

He notes that in the France attacks last month, hackers had remotely overridden the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C.

Stores had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products, with many suffering losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000). Two stores in Alsace reported a combined loss of €270,000.

The Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains were among those affected.

Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures.

In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss. They disabled alarm systems before adjusting the thermostats or extending the defrost programme by hours.

More supermarket fridge hacks reported in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg

Another hacking threat has appeared to resurface again: Supermarket operators across Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg are reporting that the temperatures in their freezers were raised overnight, leading to huge quantities of spoiled food and other damage.

We saw this sort of attack affect French supermarkets en masse last month – where the fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarchés were hacked and had their internal temperatures raised.

That led to in-store fires and a loss for supermarkets like Carrefour estimated to be in the hundreds of millions.

This morning, Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch multinational company which operates the Delhaize chain in Belgium and Luxembourg said dozens of its stores had been hit be an “IT incident’. Last month it had also reported hacks in its Albert Heijn stores in the Netherlands. It also operates supermarket chains in Greece( Alfa-Beta Vasilopoulos), Romania (Mega Image) and Serbia (Maxi).

Colruyt, which operates Spar stores in Belgium has also said five shops had their fridge systems attacked.

Swedish supermarkets ICA and Coop have also reported incidents. ICA said the freezer temperature at one store had been set to 50C, similar to the France hacks.

Russian emergency ministry app hacked hours after Ukraine attack

In Russia, authorities said this morning that hackers had gained access to the Emergency Ministry’s mobile app and sent out “fake information”.

The Emergency Ministry said it had to take the app offline temporarily but reassured residents that the wider alert system – SMS texts, broadcasts, street sirens and loudspeakers – was still in operation.

The Russian ministry didn’t say who was to blame for the attack. But Ukrainian media reported claims from Ukrainian cyber group Atesh that they were responsible for sending messages, which also contained nuclear threats.

One of the messages reportedly told residents, there was “a risk of getting lively” and warned them to “stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide”.

Belgian king 'considering' PM's resignation offer, criticises budget stall

An update in now on the Belgian PM, who’s just left the royal palace where he had a 90minute meeting with the king to offer his resignation.

The palace says that the King is “considering his decision and will consult with the party leaders of the various coalition partners starting tomorrow.”

Prime Minister Bart De Wever had offered his resignation to the king this morning after failing to pass a budget and coalition party talks breaking down last night.

The king admonished the lack of accord between politicians in the current environment of “great geopolitical uncertainty”. His statement reads:

The king regrets that no agreement has been reached on a credible budget aligned with current challenges.

In a context of great geopolitical uncertainty and significant economic challenges, the country cannot afford a prolonged political crisis.

'Disinformation as much a part of war as bombs and bullets'

Frances Mao

Back to the cyber warfare we saw last night in the app hacking in Ukraine, and then Russia.

As I noted earlier, this was direct attack on a core channel of communications between Ukrainian authorities and citizens; this app is embedded in everyday life in a war zone.

And while the full impact of the hack is still unclear – how many Ukrainians were deceived and believed the warnings for example - residents nonetheless have described how alarming it was getting a message on their phone warning of potential nuclear warfare.

Cyber-warfare expert Don Smith, from IT security firm Sophos, says these sorts of attacks are aimed at grounding down people’s mental toughness.

Disinformation is as much a part of war as bombs and bullets. Targeted information attacks could aim to impact the mental resilience of the people of Ukraine.

Their resilience is a key part of their ability to defend against the Russian military.

However he noted the ameaturish nature of this attack. One of the message sent out, in Russian, was almost jokey and casual in tone, reading: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don’t worry, it’s Oreshnik flying”, a reference to Russia’s hypersonic missiles which can pretzel and outpace most interceptors.

Usually the best information warfare is not obvious or explicit, where this very clearly is. It could indicate desperation from Russia.

Belgian PM meeting with King to tender resignation

Belgium’s prime minister Bart De Wever is handing in his resignation this morning following failed attempts to pass a budget, local media are reporting.

De Wever has been trying to get budget cuts through, and failed in late-night coalition talks yesterday to secure a compromise.

He arrived at the Royal Palace in Brussels this morning to meet with King Philippe, Belgian media say.

However they report he may be instructed to try and secure a deal again, by a certain deadline.

In Kyiv, residents received a succession of unusual alerts late on Sunday night over the period of roughly an hour.

Typically, people can receive several alerts a day warning of incoming Russian drones or missiles; locals after four years of living in a warzone are used to their phones going off, often followed by sirens in the street.

But these messages warned of radically different threats- a nuclear radiation warning, a chemical attack and even an incident of street fighting in Kyiv.

One of the messages was also transmitted in Russian, a clear tell that something was potentially off.

The messages sent out were:

22:47: “Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv.”

22:48: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don’t worry, it’s Oreshnik flying” [This message was written in Russia]

22:49: “Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don’t go outside.”

22:49: “Street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don’t go outside.”

23:53: An all clear is sent out

Ukrainian authorities within the hour had publicised messages on Telegram saying they believed the app system had been compromised.

The air raid alert channel said “unauthorised parties” had interfered with the system, which had been temporarily taken off line. It urged users to not click on links in “suspicious notifications”.

The Air Force wrote on Telegram: “The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.”

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of key events in Europe.

Ukraine and Russia have reported corresponding cyber-hacks on their app warning systems overnight.

These are the mobile apps which send alerts and air-raid warnings, alerting citizens to when missiles and drones are incoming (and thus advising residents to seek shelter or go down to a bunker).

This appears to be the first breach of the app, on such a scale, during the war so far; directly immobilising one of the most important channels of communication authorities have to help advise citizens.

In the Ukraine hack, the app started spewing out alarming fake messages late on Sunday night – warning residents of a nuclear radiation threat in the capital Kyiv, a chemical attack, street fighting and also incoming Oreshnik hypersonic missiles, which Ukraine lacks interceptors for.

Ukraine’s Air Force issued clarification within the hour on Telegram, urging people to remain calm and disregard the messages, one of which was written in Russian.

Some hours later, Russian authorities said its warning app had been hacked and had to be taken offline. A Ukrainian hacker group has claimed to have sent fake alerts warning of nuclear warheads to users inside Russia.

Amid the cyber warfare overnight, both sides also carried out strikes, targeting energy sites like oil refineries. Strikes have been reported in Zaporizhzhia and Odesa.

articles.title: Ucraina, Melania Trump: 'Evacuati da Oleshky in 800'. Hackerate le app di allarme aereo, Russia e Ucraina al buio
articles.summary: La first Lady si congratula: 'Spero che serva da base per una pace duratura'. Ma il Cremlino afferma: 'Non ci sono altre missioni umanitarie in vista'. Kiev: Raid russi su Kherson
articles.preview: La Russia ha affermato che la sua app di avvisi di emergenza è stata oggetto di un "massiccio attacco informatico", poche ore dopo che anche l'Ucraina aveva segnalato un attacco hacker ai sistemi di alert di attacchi aerei, proprio al termine della tregua più lunga tra i due Paesi in guerra. Il ministero delle emergenze di Mosca ha affermato che gli hacker hanno pubblicato "informazioni false" sull'app, progettata per avvisare il pubblico di attacchi di droni in arrivo e altre minacce.
articles.body:
La Russia ha affermato che la sua app di avvisi di emergenza è stata oggetto di un "massiccio attacco informatico", poche ore dopo che anche l'Ucraina aveva segnalato un attacco hacker ai sistemi di alert di attacchi aerei, proprio al termine della tregua più lunga tra i due Paesi in guerra.

Il ministero delle emergenze di Mosca ha affermato che gli hacker hanno pubblicato "informazioni false" sull'app, progettata per avvisare il pubblico di attacchi di droni in arrivo e altre minacce. Ore prima, l'Ucraina aveva affermato di sospettare che il suo sistema di allarme antiaereo fosse stato violato, dopo che sull'app erano apparsi avvisi infondati di una minaccia di radiazioni.

Gli attacchi informatici sono avvenuti nel momento in cui la tregua più lunga della guerra, limitata alla regione orientale di Kherson in Ucraina, è terminata ieri dopo che la Russia, secondo Kiev, ha rifiutato l'offerta di proroga. Mosca non ha immediatamente dichiarato chi si nasconde dietro l'attacco alla sua app, mentre il Centro ucraino per le comunicazioni strategiche SPRAVDI ha attribuito la responsabilità dell'hacking alla Russia.

La rara pausa nei combattimenti, mediata dalla first lady americana Melania Trump e iniziata lo scorso martedì, ha consentito una missione umanitaria nella città di Oleshky occupata dai russi. "Il cessate il fuoco, in vigore dal 27 ottobre al 1° novembre, è terminato", ha dichiarato il commissario per i diritti umani del parlamento ucraino, Dmytro Lubinets. Ha definito la tregua temporanea "un passo importante nei nostri sforzi umanitari congiunti" con la Russia.

I colloqui mediati dagli Stati Uniti tra Russia e Ucraina riprenderanno questo mese, dopo essere stati di fatto congelati da quando Stati Uniti e Israele hanno lanciato attacchi congiunti contro l'Iran a febbraio. Il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky ha detto che il suo Paese smetterebbe di colpire le raffinerie di petrolio russe - come ha chiesto la controparte americana Donald Trump - se Washington avesse fornito a Kiev potenti missili intercettori Patriot.

"Il cessate il fuoco si è concluso. La missione è stata un successo, fornendo aiuti essenziali alla regione e consentendo l'evacuazione di quasi 800 persone". Lo rende noto su X la First lady, Melania Trump, in riferimento alla tregua scattata ad Oleshky per consentire l'evacuazione di civili.

"A nome degli Stati Uniti, mi congratulo con la Russia e l'Ucraina per la loro leadership e cooperazione in merito al cessate il fuoco di Oleshky. Spero che serva da base per una pace duratura tra le due nazioni". Il cessate il fuoco è iniziato il 27 ottobre e si è concluso ieri.

Le autorità ucraine hanno riferito di una ripresa degli attacchi russi nella regione meridionale di Kherson, in seguito alla conclusione di una rara tregua localizzata che aveva consentito l'evacuazione dei residenti da una città colpita da una crisi umanitaria. "Intorno alle 8:00 di questa mattina, gli occupanti russi hanno attaccato un'auto con un drone nel quartiere di Korabelny", nella città di Kherson, provocando due feriti, ha reso noto l'amministrazione comunale su Telegram.

Le forze armate ucraine hanno probabilmente sfruttato la tregua umanitaria da Oleshky, nella regione di Kherson, per riorganizzare le proprie forze, ha dichiarato in un briefing il portavoce presidenziale russo, Dmitry Peskov. In questo modo il portavoce del Cremlino ha replicato a una richiesta di commento alle informazioni pubblicate da SkyNews, in base alle quali i russi avrebbero sfruttato il cessate il fuoco per trasportare armamenti pesanti nella città e nei villaggi circostanti.

"Possiamo presumere con un alto grado di certezza che anche le forze armate ucraine abbiano sfruttato questo periodo per un adeguato riassetto. Si tratta di una prassi del tutto normale in situazioni simili", ha affermato Peskov, citato da Interfax. Il portavoce del Cremlino ha inoltre raccomandato di contattare il ministero della Difesa russo in merito al riassetto delle truppe russe e ucraine dopo l'operazione umanitaria a Oleshki. "Tali domande dovrebbero essere rivolte al nostro dipartimento militare", ha dichiarato Peskov.

articles.preview: Un improvviso innalzamento delle temperature nei banchi frigo e freezer fino a 50 gradi ha mandato in tilt nella notte i sistemi di refrigerazione di numerosi supermercati in Svezia e Belgio, facendo temere un attacco hacker simile a quanto avvenuto in Francia il 12 ottobre scorso.Anche l'Estonia, il Lussemburgo e l'Irlanda sono state colpire da attacchi informatici ai sistemi di refrigerazione dei supermercati. articles.body:
Un improvviso innalzamento delle temperature nei banchi frigo e freezer fino a 50 gradi ha mandato in tilt nella notte i sistemi di refrigerazione di numerosi supermercati in Svezia e Belgio, facendo temere un attacco hacker simile a quanto avvenuto in Francia il 12 ottobre scorso.Anche l'Estonia, il Lussemburgo e l'Irlanda sono state colpire da attacchi informatici ai sistemi di refrigerazione dei supermercati. Lo riportano i media europei. Alcuni dei supermercati colpiti stamattina sono rimasti chiusi per gestire la crisi.

In Belgio, i cyberattacchi agli impianti di refrigerazione della grande distribuzione hanno colpito diversi punti vendita coinvolti delle principali catene del Paese, tra cui Delhaize, Carrefour, Spar e Intermarché. L'attacco ha seguito lo stesso modus operandi già osservato in Francia e ha preso di mira i sistemi di refrigerazione intorno alla mezzanotte tra domenica e lunedì. Stando a quanto riporta l'agenzia Belga disservizi si riscontrano anche presso un negozio Ikea.

"In questo momento stiamo svuotando i congelatori, non c'è molto altro che possiamo fare", ha dichiarato Dennis Vidal, il responsabile di uno dei negozi nel sud della Svezia colpiti dal problema. "Stanno ricominciando a raffreddarsi, ma è già tutto rovinato", ha aggiunto, intervistato dalla tv pubblica, Svt.

Alcuni supermercati delle catene Ica e Coop sono rimasti chiusi nelle prime ore di stamattina per gestire la crisi, ma attualmente non c'è alcuna conferma ufficiale della causa ma si teme un attacco hacker: "Siamo a conoscenza del fatto che un numero limitato di negozi è stato colpito da un incidente verificatosi durante la notte che ha compromesso i sistemi di refrigerazione e congelamento dei punti vendita", ha dichiarato, Gustaf Nilsson, portavoce dei supermercati del Gruppo Ica, riportato dall'agenzia di stampa Tt.

articles.title: Arab parties back Eisenkot: What’s the latest in Israel’s coalition talks?
articles.summary: Political wrangling is still ongoing as all blocs weigh potential paths to power.
articles.preview: Political wrangling is still ongoing as all blocs weigh potential paths to power. articles.body:
Political wrangling is still ongoing as all blocs weigh potential paths to power.

Israel’s Arab parties, which won a record-breaking 19 seats in last week’s general elections, are set to back opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc, further trampling Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s chances of leading another government.

The main Jewish opposition bloc, which includes four parties, fell short of the 61 seats needed to form a majority in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, but joining forces with the two main groups that represent Palestinian citizens of Israel could help avoid a political deadlock and another election.

Already, the “Change” opposition bloc has pledged not to join forces with Netanyahu, citing security failures that led to the October 7 Hamas attacks and an ongoing corruption trial that the prime minister faces.

But taking support from the Arab parties — whether as part of the ruling coalition or as outside support — also poses a challenge for Eisenkot from the right, at a time when leaders and parties, including Netanyahu, have been openly deploying anti-Arab racism to woo Jewish voters.

Israel’s minority Arab population has long been marginalised in politics. Since October 7, however, they have been sidelined even more. At least two former Palestinian legislators, and one current member of the Knesset, have been arrested briefly for comments or acts deemed critical of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and its occupation of the West Bank.

As the parties weigh possible paths to power, it’s likely they’ll have to make compromises and break promises made to their supporters, analysts say.

Here’s the latest:

What happened in the elections?

A coalition of Jewish conservative and far-right parties led by Prime Minister Netanyahu’s Likud won 53 seats in a Knesset of 120 seats, falling short of a majority.

The opposition bloc, led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot of the Yashar party, won 48 seats — even further away from a majority.

Meanwhile, the Arab-led Joint List and Ra’am won more seats than ever after Arab voters doubled their turnout to about 80 percent. Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, won eight seats, while the Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, won 11.

While the Arab bloc has been open to working with the opposition, there were speculations that Eisenkot would refuse their support to avoid backlash from the wider Jewish Israeli public. Arabs make up a fifth of the population of Israel. Only one Arab party, Ra’am, has successfully joined a governing coalition – in 2021. That government lasted less than two years.

Eisenkot and other opposition leaders had earlier said they would not form a coalition with Arab parties to appeal to their supporters.

What is Netanyahu saying?

Netanyahu has claimed repeatedly and without proof that Arab parties committed fraud during the elections with foreign backing.

The prime minister and his Likud party have cited a handful of cases, like the arrests of three political activists who allegedly bribed voters before polls opened. They are suspected of connections with the Ra’am party, although the party denies involvement.

Netanyahu’s case, however, appears to be weakening. On Sunday, an Israeli court released one of the suspects, and another was ordered to remain in house arrest.

Israeli election officials have also said the vote would not be undermined. Videos on Sunday of Israel’s elections chief sitting with Israel’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet intelligence service appeared to send the message that the agencies are cooperating to make the vote stand.

“Our position is that even if the suspicions are substantiated, this would not undermine the integrity of the electoral process or the election results as a whole,” Central Elections Committee head Noam Sohlberg said in the clip.

Netanyahu and Likud also suggested that the opposition bloc joining with Arab parties would be treasonous. In a statement after the vote, Likud warned that Zionist parties cooperating with the Arab bloc would be “dangerous to Israel”.

Some Israelis agree. Late on Sunday, dozens gathered outside Eisenkot’s home to protest a potential alliance.

Will Arab parties back Eisenkot?

Yes. According to several media reports, Joint List and Ra’am said they’ll collaborate with the opposition bloc to push Netanyahu out but not necessarily to form a government.

Abbas of Ra’am has long said he’d join a potential Eisenkot government if his party is given the internal security portfolio. That his deputy is a Jewish lawmaker is also seen as a signal to the opposition bloc.

Jabareen of the Joint List, meanwhile, said in a Monday interview with The Guardian that his party was ready to cooperate with the “Change” bloc to get rid of Netanyahu and other extremist members of the government, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

He clarified that the party has no intention of joining an Eisenkot government but that it would vote with it in the Knesset. That would allow Eisenkot to form a “minority government” with fewer than 61 seats.

But it’s unclear what Eisenkot and his partners will do next. The opposition bloc earlier placed conditions on any coalition with the Arab parties, saying they must accept Israel as a Jewish state, back army conscription and denounce Hamas as a terror group.

“The conditions that [Eisenkot] speaks of are more relevant for parties who would be in the coalition. We are not planning to be in the coalition … for very clear reasons,” Jabareen told The Guardian, adding that “as long as the occupation of our people in the West Bank continues, we cannot be part of a government”.

What will happen next?

The election results will be certified on Wednesday.

Afterwards, President Isaac Herzog will begin meeting with leaders of the 11 parties elected to parliament to know who they want as the next prime minister. The meeting at his residence will be livestreamed.

He will then choose the candidate he thinks is most likely to form a coalition government. As the leaders of the two main blocs, that will likely be Netanyahu or Eisenkot.

With Arab parties now expected to name Eisenkot as their preferred partner, the opposition leader could be the frontrunner to get the nod from Herzog.

Eisenkot or Netanyahu will be given 28 days to form a coalition. If that fails, the negotiation period can be extended by 14 days, after which Herzog might ask another candidate to try again.

Although chances are slim, it is still possible that Netanyahu and the opposition bloc could enter talks and agree to form a unity government. Or Netanyahu could attempt to pull at least eight members of the opposition bloc.

Already, Yashar claimed in an X post on Saturday that several of its members had gotten calls from Likud, which it said was in a state of “hysteria”.

Meanwhile, parliamentarians will be sworn in on November 10 regardless of the coalition talks.

articles.title: How US oil firms profit $130bn from Iran war as household bills surge
articles.summary: As energy from the Gulf and Russia take a hit, American oil and gas firms are the big gainers.
articles.preview: As energy from the Gulf and Russia take a hit, American oil and gas firms are the big gainers. The biggest losers: consumers around the world. United States oil companies have earned more than $130bn in profits during the war on Iran, even as consumers pay much higher prices for key commodities, amid fears that US President Donald Trump may renew fighting after midterm elections.
articles.body:
As energy from the Gulf and Russia take a hit, American oil and gas firms are the big gainers. The biggest losers: consumers around the world.

United States oil companies have earned more than $130bn in profits during the war on Iran, even as consumers pay much higher prices for key commodities, amid fears that US President Donald Trump may renew fighting after midterm elections.

The estimate, released by The New York Times, is a conservative evaluation based on the performance of 51 large US oil and gas companies in the six months from April through September. By contrast, in the same period in 2025 – when the prices of oil were lower prior to the launch of the US-Israel war on Iran – they collectively earned less than $47bn.

But the gains come as burgeoning living costs are crushing consumers. Americans have spent an extra $150bn on petrol and diesel since the war on Iran began on February 28, according to an analysis by Brown University’s Climate Solutions Lab, which amounts to more than $1,150 per household.

The disparity has fuelled a political debate over who gains and who pays the price for the war. Responding to Trump, Democratic Representative Jim McGovern wrote on X: “We’re not making a ‘freaking fortune,’ we’re PAYING a ‘freaking fortune’.”

US Big Oil in position to profit where others lose

Naser al-Tamimi, a fellow at the Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI) in Milan, Italy, said US energy companies have benefitted from the war in different ways. “Crude producers gain from higher oil prices, while refiners capture exceptional margins as diesel and other fuel supplies tighten,” he said.

Additionally, “damage to Middle Eastern and Russian refineries, disrupted Strait of Hormuz shipments, and sanctions-related trade frictions have intensified shortages”, while “relatively secure US facilities and access to discounted crude strengthen these gains”.

ExxonMobil and Chevron, the biggest US oil companies, on Friday reported profits of between $10bn and $15bn. While the gains are considerable, The New York Times found they generally remained below 2022 levels, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused oil prices to soar to roughly $100 a barrel and raised natural gas prices, compared with the current average of $90 from April through September.

American refining companies also reaped greater profits as global fuel supplies tightened and inventories depleted due to heavy damage to infrastructure in the Middle East and Russia. Valero Energy’s third-quarter profit increased more than sixfold, reaching $6.83bn. Phillips 66 announced its highest quarterly profit on record, with net income jumping to $5.62bn from $133m a year earlier.

Geoffrey Miller, geopolitical analyst and editor of the Gulf States Insights newsletter, said the US-Israel war with Iran “created the largest supply-side shock to global oil and refined products markets in years”.

Miller added that the war “created a risk premium that US-based operators are structurally well placed to monetise”. By contrast, Gulf producers were “hit hard by both higher costs and risks, along with physical damage, which makes their ability to benefit from the higher prices much more difficult”.

Tehran retaliated against the US-Israeli attack by launching missiles and drones at the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC). The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), a US-registered independent conflict monitor, found Iran and Iran-backed groups in the region have carried out at least 172 attacks on nonmilitary infrastructure across the six GCC member states. Despite claims by Iranian officials that they were targeting US military facilities, they also hit energy infrastructure.

Iran also effectively blocked passage of most vessels through the Strait of Hormuz. In retaliation, the US imposed a naval blockade on Iranian oil and gas – the tit-for-tat steps raising the risks of transporting energy out of the crucial passageway.

Continued pressure over cost of living

Analysts warned of continued volatility until a durable political settlement between the US and Iran is reached. Oil prices dropped briefly in the summer after a memorandum of understanding was signed in June, but prices quickly soared again when talks broke down.

A more recent escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has further compounded the crisis: the Bab al-Mandeb strait that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, which Saudi Arabia uses to export oil, is now also a theatre of war.

“In the short term, windfall profits will only strengthen oil company balance sheets and shareholder returns,” Miller said. “However, the big profits come with a major caveat. That’s because over the longer term, high oil prices risk harming economic growth prospects and could even contribute towards the outbreak of a recession, which would in turn be likely to lead to reduced demand for oil” and accelerate the transition to renewable energy.

Florence Schmit, senior energy strategist at Rabobank’s global economics and markets team in London, said it was likely that the prices of key energy products would remain high given the uncertainty about the duration of the war in Iran.

“Prices in all markets that have an exposure to this global supply shock – which includes the US – will face high prices also next year, and consumers will continue to feel this price pressure unless governments step in,” Schmit told Al Jazeera.

The US-led war on Iran has raised costs for oil, transport fuels, gas, electricity and food. According to the World Bank Group’s latest Commodity Markets Outlook, commodity prices are set to rise 23 percent this year, as disrupted grain shipments and the El Nino weather phenomenon also threaten harvests and food affordability.

The United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization said on October 2 that world food commodity prices rose a further 1.5 percent in September, after reaching their highest level since late 2022 in August, amid adverse weather and trade disruptions in the Black Sea and Strait of Hormuz.

Trump has sought to blame high global fuel prices on Ukraine and pressured Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian refineries, even as Moscow continued to wage attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The US president has argued that a deal with Russia reversing years of sanctions would help lower diesel prices.

In the Gulf, analysts said higher oil prices will benefit exporters that can maintain shipments, but prolonged insecurity will continue to threaten supply reliability and investment.

“Gulf producers face years of reconstruction and pressure to diversify export routes,” ISPI’s al-Tamimi said. “A diplomatic settlement could ease prices, whereas renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran risk triggering another regional war, further disrupting Hormuz and prolonging shortages.”

articles.body:
Iran has retained significant offensive capability, but civilians and critical infrastructure remain largely exposed.

Tehran, Iran – Iran’s military is warning that if all-out war breaks out again with the United States and Israel, it will be longer and more costly than their rivals expect.

Iran’s armed forces could deploy new weapons and tactics against the US, Israel and other countries, which would be the third major conflict between the countries since June last year.

There have been increasing signs that the US and Israel’s war on Iran, which began on February 28, could restart after the US midterm elections. President Donald Trump said on Sunday that the war with Iran will end “very soon one way or the other” and Tehran should agree a deal or “the hammer” will come down.

Hossein Kanani Moghaddam, a former senior IRGC commander, told Al Jazeera that despite extensive blows to the Iranian armed forces during US and Israeli strikes earlier this year, they are now in better operational shape compared with previous conflicts.

“In terms of offence, our target database has significantly expanded, the range, accuracy and warheads of our missiles have improved and our drone capabilities have increased,” he said.

New enemy assets were being identified and operations in additional geographical areas were being planned, he added. Arkaminia said that previously undisclosed capabilities and targets would be revealed – and used – if Iran is attacked again.

Commanders from Iran’s General Staff of Armed Forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Islamic Republic of Iran Army are reported to have recently met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to discuss what steps will be taken if attacked again. The response will be immediate and could go beyond the West Asia region, they said.

The IRGC was “100 percent ready” to confront another attack, spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said on Sunday evening, describing “maximum deterrence” as a goal Iran would reach in the near future.

Army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said the commanders would rely on “asymmetric warfare” tactics that would compensate for the superiority of US military equipment.

He added that “some weaponry was renovated and new equipment was added along with new tactics” during the brief ceasefire period that came after the June memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US.

Last month, state television showed an underground drone production line. The authorities also showcased an upgraded version of the Arash attack drone and claimed that its warhead had doubled to 100kg with improved guidance.

According to a Reuters investigation published last week, numerous military agencies linked with Iran’s defence establishment have evaded sanctions and funnelled billions into military imports to replenish the IRGC. The imports between January 2025 and June this year from China, Russia and Germany to fuel missile and drone production included rocket propellants, explosives, detonators, titanium and heavy-duty trucks that could be used as launchers.

Many Iranian missile defence systems, radars and other equipment were hit during the war. But Kanani Moghaddam said remaining and newly developed systems were becoming more accurate, pointing to the targeting of a US-built F-35 and other warplanes and drones as successes that can be replicated and expanded upon.

“At sea, we have shown that we can easily target supertankers,” he said regarding transit through the Strait of Hormuz that is deemed “unauthorised” by Iranian authorities. He said Iranian attacks on US Navy vessels in September prompted them to stop venturing into the critical waterway since. But the US has continued its naval blockade on southern Iranian ports, while Iran’s civilian population and infrastructure remain largely exposed if the war resumes.

Tehran and other cities across the country lack shelters or early warning systems to protect civilians. Authorities have not reported any progress regarding the promised shelters and gaps in public warning arrangements.

Iran’s electricity grid, as well as oil and gas facilities, petrochemical and steel manufacturers and roads and railways could also be attacked again, making life even more difficult amid the economic crisis.

‘Intelligence weakness’

During both wars, many senior political and military figures of the Islamic Republic were killed by US and Israeli strikes.

The new supreme leader has not been seen or heard from since replacing his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in early March, ostensibly for security reasons.

This has led to tighter domestic security controls, and prompted some voices from within the establishment to raise concerns and demand accountability for intelligence failures and protection of leadership.

“We have been hit and hit hard,” state-linked analyst Hamzeh Rahim Safavi said during a televised debate on Saturday. “The main cause is intelligence weakness, but no one talks about it or is held accountable”.

The analyst is the son of Yahya Rahim Safavi, a former commander-in-chief of the IRGC who currently serves as a senior military adviser to the supreme leader. The analyst said calls by hardliners to acquire a nuclear bomb would not repair intelligence and security weaknesses.

But Esmaeil Kowsari, a former IRGC division commander now a parliamentary national-security commission member, told local media last week that even though the supreme leader and others were assassinated, “the enemies did not reach their main goals”. He said the goals were to overthrow the Islamic Republic and fragment Iran.

“On the eve of their elections, the Americans are trying to pretend that they have achieved victory by causing a ruckus and launching psychological operations, but that is not the truth,” Kowsari said.

articles.body:
A New South Wales local council has refused to show a world-renowned artwork about children killed in Gaza after asking organisers to investigate hiring “armed guards” to counter the risk of “community conflict” over the mural.

The group, Shoalhaven Friends of Palestine, was aiming to show the Wall of Tears installation by American artist Phil Buehler at the Shoalhaven Regional Gallery in Nowra on Tuesday, following the work being exhibited around Australia, including on the front lawns of Parliament House in Canberra in September.

The massive artwork pays homage to the 18,457 children killed in Gaza between 7 October 2023 and 19 July 2025 and was first shown in New York on 29 January to coincide with the second anniversary of the death of Hind Rajab, a five-year-old left to bleed out among the bodies of six family members after their car was targeted by an Israeli tank.

Shoalhaven city council asked the group to “investigate” the use of “armed guards” in a risk assessment seen by Guardian Australia. The perceived risks included “protest, counter-protest, community conflict,” and “verbal abuse, intimidation or disruption arising from politically sensitive subject matter”.

The group was also asked to reduce the exhibition window from eight days to three days and restrict attendance to RSVPs only in the gallery, which would have “locked doors”.

Organisers were also requested to no longer advertise the event due to potential “reputational risk” for the gallery or council due to their decision to host the exhibition.

“We were like, ‘You’ve got to be kidding me,’ but we still wrote back to them and said we would meet all the requirements you want,” said Annette Pham, a member of the group.

“We didn’t even know where we could get armed guards, or if you could get them.”

Despite this, email correspondence shows Andrew Constance – the chief executive of the council and former Liberal MP – decided against hosting the event, citing staff safety concerns.

Pham wrote to the council stating she was “deeply disappointed” by the decision and said the “very suggestion that armed guards might be necessary for an exhibition commemorating dead children is deeply disturbing”.

“We are organising a memorial art exhibition, not an event for which Council has disclosed any specific credible threat of violence requiring consideration of armed protection and metal screening,” Pham wrote in her email.

A council spokesperson said in a statement that they had considered the request, but “the installation was deemed to present an unacceptable level of risk to gallery staff, visitors and tenants of the building”.

The council did not respond directly to a question from Guardian Australia about what had triggered the safety concerns.

Pham has now arranged for the work to be installed at Berry Uniting Church on Thursday.

‘They’re children’

Buehler said he was shocked his artwork, which has been shown in cities around the world, could be perceived as posing a safety risk.

“They’re children. They’re like your children, my children,” he said, adding it refers to death toll figures accepted by Israel. The artwork draws from Guardian reporting.

“If you look at the pictures on that mural … There’s kids in their little graduation outfits holding diplomas, they’re holding soccer balls. They’re there with their siblings, or on their father’s shoulder. It was the hardest artwork I’ve ever made, to just live with [what happened to these children], for the time it took to make it.”

“If people would just look at that, how can that be dangerous? The danger is put on by other people who are trying to turn it into something it’s not.”

The artwork has been touring around Australia, including in Adelaide where it was first shown, and Perth where it was shown at the Western Australian state parliament.

Dr Mairead Heaney is part of Perth Doctors Medical Aid for Palestine which helped arrange the exhibition at the WA parliament and the federal Parliament House in Canberra.

She said a number of Labor, Greens and independent MPs visited the artwork when it was displayed in Canberra, including Labor MP Tony Zappia, who made a statement to parliament about it.

Zappia said in his speech: “The banner is a sad reminder of the level of Palestinian human losses, suffering, and daily violations they endure, while much of the world looks away.”

"The possibility of implementing this plan in two days is another indication of Iran's good-faith approach," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters at a briefing.

articles.body:
Ryanair has said it is considering implementing pay freezes, setting the scene for a confrontation with unions as the airline tries to offset soaring fuel costs driven by the Middle East conflict.

The airline is also considering reducing crew numbers on flights and increasing the use of AI, in a cost-cutting drive.

Europe’s largest low-cost carrier said it expected European airlines to raise ticket prices by up to 20%, with its own jet fuel costs forecast to rise by about €2bn (£1.6bn) in its next financial year, which ends in March 2028.

“Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict we expect jet fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027,” said Michael O’Leary, the chief executive of Ryanair. “While we believe European short-haul fares will increase materially to reflect these much higher jet-fuel prices and competitor capacity reductions, this is unlikely to provide a full offset for an estimated €2bn increase in our fuel bill.”

Oil prices hit a six-month high on Friday before falling to about $106 a barrel on Monday.

Ryanair expects European short-haul fares to “increase materially” next year, as fuel hedging deals taken out by airlines to reduce costs expire.

“To help address this, we’re reviewing all costs across group airlines with a particular focus on airport churn negotiations, maturing labour agreements (which may require temporary pay freezes), lower crew ratios and increased use of AI,” O’Leary said.

He said the company had several pay deals that would come up for renegotiation from March.

However, the Unite union said it had a multiyear pay deal in place that covered 2027, and in any case was not linked to company performance.

“Unite hasn’t been advised of any such proposals and we have a multiyear pay deal in place which covers next year,” said Oliver Richardson, a national officer at the union. “A number of unions across Europe have the same. Our pay agreement was not attached to, nor dependent on company performance. This was something that the Ryanair was at pains to emphasise. As such we would expect it to be honoured.”

O’Leary also said Ryanair was “slowing down hiring meaningfully” for new pilots, cabin crew and across its training courses.

The company said its increased use of AI would focus on improving productivity in operations and back-office and support functions.

O’Leary said AI had already been used to increase capacity by 4%.

“When you’re running 650 aircraft, it’s too big for a human to be able to do it,” he said. “The machines can actually design the schedules better than we know [how to do], so we are getting more productivity out of the aircraft.”

Ryanair said 80% of its fuel requirements until the end of March were hedged at $67 a barrel. Twenty-five per cent of its fuel requirements for the subsequent 12 months are hedged at $95 a barrel.

“It’s beginning to dawn on everybody that we [the industry] are not well hedged,” O’Leary said.

The Irish airline, Europe’s largest by passenger numbers, said average fares fell by 2% year on year in the quarter ending in September. Ryanair added that fares in the final three months of the year were trending “modestly ahead” of the same quarter last year.

“The booking window remains closer-in which reduces visibility,” the company said. “[The current quarter’s] fare outcome will heavily depend on the strength of close-in October-November school midterm [holiday] and Christmas bookings.”

The airline reported a post-tax profit of €1.61bn in the quarter ending in September, a fall of 6% year on year but in line with analyst expectations. Passenger numbers grew 5% year on year to 64.5 million during the quarter.

Ryanair has taken delivery of about 30 aircraft annually over the last two years, but the delivery rate is set to drop to 15 annually for the next few years.

The airline said it was to take deliveries of the Boeing 737 Max 10 aircraft in January, which has about 20% more seats but burns a fifth less fuel than its current fleet.

articles.title: Will renewed conflict derail Ethiopia's economic growth?
articles.summary: Ethiopia's economy is growing strongly. But renewed fighting in the north of the BRICS member state could deter investment, strain public finances and push up the cost of living.

articles.body:
November 2, 2026

Ethiopia's economy is growing strongly. But renewed fighting in the north of the BRICS member state could deter investment, strain public finances and push up the cost of living.

Ethiopia's economy is growing strongly. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts real growth of 9.2% for the 2025–26 fiscal year. But renewed fighting in the north, high reconstruction costs and climate-related crop problems are threatening the country's economic recovery.

London-based financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed warns of the consequences of further escalation. "If there is a major conflict [...] the current economic growth will not be sustainable," he told DW.

The costly legacy of the Tigray war

The war that raged in Tigray and other parts of Ethiopia between 2020 and 2022 inflicted extensive damage. Infrastructure was destroyed, businesses lost production capacity and agricultural land could no longer be cultivated in some areas.

A World Bank-backed damage and needs assessment puts the damage caused by several conflicts in Ethiopia between November 2020 and December 2021 at more than $22.6 billion (€20.2 billion). Economic losses amounted to around $6 billion. The estimated bill for reconstruction and economic recovery stands at approximately $19.7 billion, which covers the total funding needed, not annual costs or damage caused by the current escalation.

A reconstruction plan covered the period from 2023 to 2028. However, it remains uncertain whether the work can be fully funded and completed within that timeframe.

Financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed believes the economic consequences of the Tigray war were even more severe. In addition to the direct destruction, he points to lost economic output, high inflation and foreign currency shortages at the time. International trade conditions also deteriorated: in 2022, Ethiopia lost its benefits under the US African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which had allowed certain African exports to enter the US market duty-free.

Growth despite the crisis

Following the Pretoria peace agreement in November 2022, the economy began to recover. According to the IMF, it grew by 7.2% in 2022–23 and 8.1% in 2023–24. The organization puts growth at 9.2% for 2024–25 and forecasts a further 9.2% for 2025–26. Agriculture, mining and electricity generation are among the main drivers.

This does not contradict the economic damage caused by the war. Gross domestic product (GDP) measures the total economic output of a country. If major sectors outside conflict-affected areas continue to expand, the overall economy can grow even while individual regions are still suffering the consequences of violence.

However, high growth rates do not mean that the country's economic problems have been resolved. Reconstruction remains a major challenge, inflation continues to put pressure on households and the government has to service its debt. In late 2023, Ethiopia defaulted after missing an interest payment on a Eurobond. Reforms supported by an IMF program launched in 2024 are intended to address structural weaknesses in the economy.

More military spending, less money for development

A renewed escalation could put additional pressure on public finances. The government would have to spend more on military personnel, equipment and logistics. At the same time, economic activity and, consequently, tax revenues could decline in the affected regions.

"A substantial share of government resources would be tied up in military spending that would otherwise be available for infrastructure, education and social services," warned Abdulmenan Mohammed. The extent of this impact would depend on the scale and duration of any renewed conflict.

A prolonged war could also prompt businesses to postpone investments. International lenders and donors might become more cautious, while the government would need additional funds for security and humanitarian assistance. This could leave less money available for roads, energy infrastructure and other development projects.

Inflation and foreign currency shortages

The IMF forecasts an average inflation rate of 11.7% for 2025–26. Prices are therefore expected to continue rising, although at a slower pace than in previous years.

Abdulmenan Mohammed expects a further escalation to intensify inflationary pressures. "If the conflict escalates further, inflation is likely to rise," he said. To finance additional spending, the government might resort to more domestic borrowing. This could crowd out private businesses by making it harder for them to access credit and finance investments.

The military also needs foreign currency to purchase equipment from abroad. If this demand increases, fewer foreign exchange reserves could be available to private businesses for imports. This would put further pressure on the birr exchange rate and drive up the cost of imported goods, fuel and industrial inputs.

The extent of these effects on the BRICS member state would also depend on export earnings, monetary policy and developments in international markets. A new surge in inflation is therefore a risk, but not an inevitable consequence of the escalation. A combination of rising prices and uncertain incomes would be particularly difficult for poorer households.

Agriculture and tourism particularly vulnerable

Abdulmenan Mohammed sees agriculture, as well as the tourism and hospitality sectors, as particularly vulnerable. "Agriculture is especially exposed because much of the fighting takes place in rural areas where farmers work," he said.

Insecurity around farmland, disrupted transport routes and shortages of agricultural inputs can undermine production. At the same time, parts of the country are experiencing insufficient rainfall and poor harvest prospects. Failed harvests reduce farmers' incomes, while lower food supplies can push prices even higher.

Tourism is also highly sensitive to security risks. Travel advisories and reports of fighting can deter visitors, reducing revenues for hotels and tour operators.

Could neighboring countries benefit from the crisis?

When making investment decisions, international investors consider not only market size but also political stability, security and the reliability of state institutions. A further escalation could therefore delay investment decisions or prompt companies to consider alternative locations.

However, there is currently no concrete evidence that companies are already withdrawing investments from Ethiopia because of the fighting and relocating them to neighboring countries such as Kenya. Abdulmenan Mohammed also sees no demonstrable economic advantage for Kenya at this stage. Beyond security, factors such as tax administration, public services and governance also play a decisive role.

This article was originally published in German.

Somaliland

Israel’s first ambassador to Somaliland has presented his credentials to President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, known as Cirro, in Hargeisa. The ceremony also marked the laying of the cornerstone for an Israeli embassy.

Israel recognised Somaliland in December 2025, becoming the first United Nations member state to do so. Somaliland declared independence from Somalia in 1991, but Mogadishu continues to claim the territory, which has not been recognised by any other UN member state.

Cirro called the occasion historic, while Ambassador Michael Lotem said the recognition acknowledged what Somaliland had built over 35 years. Israel’s foreign minister said the exchange of ambassadors fulfilled commitments made when diplomatic relations were established.

The relationship has drawn criticism from Somalia, the Arab League, the African Union and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud accused Israel of seeking access to the Red Sea and alleged it wanted a naval base in Somaliland. Somaliland officials have indicated openness to hosting an Israeli military base, though Cirro recently said no talks had taken place.

"The Middle East Gulf region should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict. Peace and stability in the region require joint nurturing and protection by all parties," says Chinese President Xi Jinping.

BEIJING: The Middle East and Gulf region should not become a battleground for great-power rivalry and China is willing to work with Arab nations to achieve lasting peace, Chinese President Xi Jinping told Oman's sultan on Monday (Nov 2).

China has traditionally played a low-key diplomatic role in the Middle East, but has stepped up efforts to try to help end tensions amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has snarled the Strait of Hormuz and driven up global energy and shipping costs.

Xi told Omani Sultan Haitham bin Tariq al-Said that the world is undergoing profound changes.

"The Middle East Gulf region should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict. Peace and stability in the region require joint nurturing and protection by all parties," Xi said, according to China's Foreign Ministry.

China has consistently been committed to stopping the war, and hopes to contribute "wisdom and solutions to resolving the region's security dilemmas", he added.

China is willing to strengthen communication and coordination with Arab countries, including the Gulf Cooperation Council states, to work together toward restoring peace and achieving lasting stability and security, Xi said.

In a 20-point joint statement, both sides said they agree that normal and safe navigation should resume in the Strait of Hormuz. The countries also called for the US and Iran to pursue peaceful options, return to the agreement struck in June aimed at ending the conflict and restart dialogue.

Separately, China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi said on Monday that all parties in the Middle East conflict should focus on political solutions rather than resorting to arms again, in a meeting with an Iranian national security official in Beijing.

Dialogue and negotiation are the way to resolve Middle East conflicts, Wang told Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy secretary of the Iran Supreme National Security Council, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.

Wang also said China supports Iran in safeguarding its sovereignty and security.

China, which is pressing for a bigger diplomatic role in the Middle East, also announced that its special envoy to the Middle East, would visit Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia this month.

FIRST CHINA TRIP

Haitham arrived in Beijing on Sunday for a two-day visit, the first by an Omani head of state since the countries established ties in 1978.

Haitham told Xi his government had deep appreciation for China's positions on key issues concerning the region, Omani state media reported.

"We believe that development and stability are inextricably linked," he said.

"The prosperity of nations requires an environment defined by security, peace, respect for state sovereignty, and adherence to international law — an environment where disputes are resolved through peaceful means."

Chinese President Xi Jinping has offered to help protect maritime shipping in the Middle East amid the turmoil due to the US war on Iran. He made the offer as he met his Egyptian counterpart Abdel Fattah al-Sisi in Cairo. It's his first trip to Egypt in a decade. Rebecca Metteo reports from Beijing.

He also said Oman was open to entering into a preferential bilateral trade and investment agreement with China.

"We are confident that such an agreement would open new avenues for trade and investment, facilitate and enhance commercial and investment exchanges between our two nations," Haitham said.

China is Oman's largest trade partner, with tourism and business links boosted by direct flights between Beijing and Muscat since November last year.

Oman, which exports crude oil and energy products to China, has also been looking to further develop its renewable energy supply chains and digital commerce.

The Omani leader, who was welcomed on the tarmac in Beijing by People's Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng, also emphasised cooperation between investment and financial institutions.

articles.title: Inneggiare ad Hamas è reato?
articles.summary: Secondo il leader di Rifondazione Comunista Maurizio Acerbo, inneggiare all’organizzazione palestinese o agli attacchi del 7 ottobre sarebbe «assolutamente lecito», ma le cose non stanno sempre così
