Il 26 ottobre, il segretario di Rifondazione Comunista Maurizio Acerbo ha posto questa domanda su X, rispondendo a un utente che accusava l’attivista Youssef Siher, coinvolto nelle indagini sui disordini avvenuti a Milano il 17 e 18 ottobre, di essere un sostenitore dell’organizzazione palestinese. Acerbo ha poi aggiunto: «Inneggiare al 7 ottobre non è un reato. C’è chi inneggia a Israele e chi inneggia a Hamas. In una democrazia è assolutamente lecito».
articles.body:
«Quindi? È vietato inneggiare a Hamas?». Il 26 ottobre, il segretario di Rifondazione Comunista Maurizio Acerbo ha posto questa domanda su X, rispondendo a un utente che accusava l’attivista Youssef Siher, coinvolto nelle indagini sui disordini avvenuti a Milano il 17 e 18 ottobre, di essere un sostenitore dell’organizzazione palestinese. Acerbo ha poi aggiunto: «Inneggiare al 7 ottobre non è un reato. C’è chi inneggia a Israele e chi inneggia a Hamas. In una democrazia è assolutamente lecito».

Le dichiarazioni hanno suscitato un acceso dibattito politico. Successivamente Acerbo ha precisato di non sostenere Hamas, rivendicando il diritto di esprimere liberamente le proprie opinioni.

Ma che cosa prevede l’ordinamento italiano? In breve, la Costituzione tutela la libertà di manifestare anche le idee più radicali e controverse. Tuttavia, questa libertà incontra alcuni limiti. In particolare, l’esaltazione pubblica di un’organizzazione che l’Unione europea considera come terroristica o dei delitti da essa commessi può costituire reato quando, per il contenuto delle dichiarazioni e il contesto in cui vengono rese, sia concretamente idonea a favorire la commissione di ulteriori delitti. Pertanto, inneggiare ad Hamas non è automaticamente un reato, ma non è nemmeno sempre lecito.

articles.body:
Patti Zirhut, a lifelong Republican, has been studying her ballot for weeks. Zirhut eagerly voted for President Donald Trump in 2016, 2020, and 2024, but she isn’t toeing the party line this year. “My ballot is all mixed up,” she says. She’s voting for some Republicans, some independents, and even a few Democrats. Zirhut remains undecided on a few races, but of one thing she is absolutely certain: “I will not vote for Byron Donalds,” she tells me. “No way will I ever vote for him.”

Bipartisan outrage has been growing for months — but Republicans’ many advantages could still help them win.

Donalds, the Republican nominee in Florida’s gubernatorial election, has Trump’s endorsement, the party’s backing, and $148 million in campaign funds, much of it from the tech industry. It’s this latest point that particularly rankles Zirhut, an organizer with a group called No Data Center Hernando County, whose purpose is summed up in its name. Donalds has been a vocal supporter of the controversial developments — a fact that may now cost him votes, even among members of his own party.

I first met Zirhut in August at a small protest in the rural community of Spring Hill, Florida. Back then, Donalds was the front-runner in a crowded Republican primary, and Zirhut told me she wouldn’t vote for him if he won. Now Donalds is the nominee in a race that is much closer than anyone anticipated, and Zirhut is sticking to her word. “I’m disgusted with all these dirty politics,” she tells me. She’s thinking about voting for Donalds’ Democratic opponent, former Rep. David Jolly.

Jolly, a former Republican who left the party in 2018, is now hoping to win over newly disgruntled conservatives like Zirhut — and his stance on data centers may help him do it. In Florida, the opposition to data centers “is more intense among Republicans than it is among Democrats,” Jolly tells The Verge, “because it is a reflection of the outsized influence and control of Big Tech and Big Data in a world where people are worried about surveillance, whether it’s AI or development encroaching on their land and their freedom.”

When it comes to data centers, the differences between Donalds and Jolly couldn’t be more stark. Jolly has traveled to Virginia’s Loudoun County, also known as Data Center Alley, to “see what massive hyperscale data centers really do to a community.” Donalds has said he wants to “make Florida the financial capital of the world.” Jolly has promised to implement a one-year moratorium on data center developments. Donalds has said he wants to welcome the tech industry — including data center developers — to the Sunshine State. “There ain’t no bans coming,” Donalds said in August. “But it sounds good on TV, or it sounds good on social media.” Donalds has since moderated his stance on data centers, trying to appeal to the 68 percent of Floridians who say they oppose the developments in their communities.

“This is an opportunity you rarely see in politics for candidates to both lead and follow,” Jolly says. “If 70 percent of the state is saying ‘Don’t do it,’ the job is to listen to voters, not to tell voters they’re wrong. But there are policy reasons, as well, to lead in this moment.”

Jolly rattled off a litany of reasons to slow down, if not altogether halt, data center development in Florida: air and noise pollution; the public health effects on people who live near data centers’ on-site power plants; and environmental concerns including water use, an issue he acknowledged is partly mitigated by the move to closed-loop air cooling. He also pointed to the rapid development of AI technology, which is advancing so quickly that facilities built today “may well be functionally obsolete in the next 10 years.”

When it comes to data centers, the differences between Donalds and Jolly couldn’t be more stark.

Donalds is quick to point out that his running mate, state Sen. Bryan Ávila, sponsored a bill regulating new data center projects that requires them to pay their fair share for water and electricity. And he’s emphasized that these developments ultimately aren’t the governor’s purview. “When it comes to data centers and local control, local governments are going to have the final say,” Donalds recently told CBS News. “Governors don’t issue building permits; local governments do. So if a local community does not want a data center, then no data centers.” But Jolly has saddled his opponent with a nickname that sums up their differences on the issue: “Data Center Donalds.” Donalds’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Raul Alfonso, the chair of Watchdogs of Fort Meade, a community group fighting a $2.6 billion hyperscale data center development in deep-red Polk County, said his group has reached out to candidates in the lead-up to the election. Earlier this year, Watchdogs of Fort Meade received what Alfonso describes as a “form letter” from both Donalds and from Ron DeSantis, Florida’s current Republican governor. “It was basically, ‘We have to trust that your local city commissioners and your local city representatives will do the right thing,’” he says. The group hasn’t heard back from Jolly — which doesn’t bother Alfonso much, given Jolly’s promised moratorium. James Fishback, the controversial Republican contender who ended up with 10 percent of the primary vote, was the first to respond. Bobby Williams, a Republican candidate who garnered just 4.1 percent of the vote, has attended several events. Angie Nixon, the Democrat running to unseat Sen. Ashley Moody, hosted a town hall in Fort Meade to discuss residents’ opposition to the data centers. For Alfonso, the difference comes down to a willingness to hear locals’ concerns. Nixon, a Democratic Socialist, has little in common with the far-right Fishback, but both have engaged with the locals fighting the Fort Meade data center in a way Donalds hasn’t.

“There are a lot of people that were deep-red individuals who voted party line all the way, who are looking at flopping over to somebody who will actually take the concerns of the citizens more seriously,” Alfonso says. Alfonso’s voting history skews conservative — he voted for Trump in 2016, 2020, and 2024 — but he was a registered independent until this year, when he switched his affiliation to Republican to vote for Williams in the primary.

Williams, a pastor who had not previously run for office, has since endorsed Jolly. “The Republican Party, they kind of selected their nominee. They had their guy from the get-go: Donalds,” Williams tells me. “Big corporations are obviously buying a lot of these seats. They’re buying the governor’s role.” For Williams, data center developers are the latest in a long list of outsiders that want to have their way with Florida.

If he wins, Jolly will be the first Democratic governor Florida has elected in 28 years. The polls are close. One recent survey conducted by the University of North Florida put Jolly just two points behind Donalds, within the 2.8 percent margin of error. Donalds has several advantages over Jolly, not least of which is money. Jolly has raised $22 million to Donalds’ $148 million. There’s also the fact that Florida, once a swing state, now has nearly 2 million more registered Republicans than Democrats, in part because of DeSantis’ response to the covid-19 pandemic. The fact that Republicans currently lead Democrats in early voting may suggest that the state is unlikely to flip. But some of those Republicans, including Zirhut, are wary of Donald’s support for — and from — the tech industry, and are voting accordingly. Donalds has received $5 million from Leading the Future, a pro-AI super PAC whose funders include executives of OpenAI, Palantir, and Andreessen Horowitz.

As vocal as data center opponents may be, these developments aren’t Florida voters’ main issue. Poll after poll has shown that in Florida and elsewhere, the cost of living is top of mind for voters of all political orientations. But Jolly says the mass opposition to data centers is a manifestation of voters’ broader concerns.

“It’s almost a physical metaphor for anxieties around, ‘What is the future of work? What’s the future of wages? What does this mean for security and privacy for myself and for my kids?’” Jolly says. The huge sums of money spent on the governor’s race, he adds, are a testament to economic inequality in a state with an ever-rising cost of living. “In a state like Florida with unlimited money, where people feel like they’ve lost their political and economic power and voice, the deepest-pocketed special interests — be it tech, data, utilities — are able to capture our politicians and decision-making.”

The ChatGPT desktop app can be a confusing piece of software, given that there are ChatGPT and Codex sections, and within the former, there are Chat and Work tabs. With so many options, it’s sometimes easy to forget where you are working and where exactly your project is.

“This will enable you to move from exploring an idea to having ChatGPT carry it through, all in one place. Codex will remain a separate experience in the ChatGPT desktop app,” the email said.

Rival Anthropic merged Claude’s chat and Cowork functions into one screen in September.

articles.title: Ford launches a ‘privacy promise’ and explains how and why it uses customer data
articles.summary: Ford said it's making an "explicit commitment" to its customers that "their vehicle data is safe" with the company.
articles.preview: As Ford prepares to launch a new generation of connected cars, the automaker is making a public promise about how it will handle that information. The company unveiled on Monday what it calls a “privacy promise” — an “explicit commitment” to keep customers’ vehicle data safe and give them control over what they share. Ford also launched a website designed to educate customers about how, where, and why the automakers uses their data, and to show them how to change those settings.
articles.body:
As Ford prepares to launch a new generation of connected cars, the automaker is making a public promise about how it will handle that information.

The company unveiled on Monday what it calls a “privacy promise” — an “explicit commitment” to keep customers’ vehicle data safe and give them control over what they share. Ford also launched a website designed to educate customers about how, where, and why the automakers uses their data, and to show them how to change those settings.

While those controls have existed for years now, Ford wants to communicate more clearly with its customers about them, especially ahead of the launch of new, more connected vehicles like the ones being built on its upcoming “universal electric vehicle” platform.

“I personally think that it’s super important for us to be making it very clear to our customers what our data practices are, and not only that, but making a commitment to them about it,” Ford’s chief privacy officer Kristin Jones said in an interview with TechCrunch. “I also see this as a great opportunity to educate our customers about how they share data.”

This new privacy push comes as automakers are making their cars increasingly connected. While some polling shows U.S. customers want the kinds of features enabled by this connectivity, such as remote start, navigation, and driver-assistance software, only 14% said they fully understand what data their vehicle collects.

That has left room for some companies to quietly sell that data to third parties — a practice that got General Motors in trouble with the Federal Trade Commission, and also resulted in a $220 million settlement with 36 states last week.

This lack of consumer awareness around data collection and sharing has also opened the door for other companies to market themselves as better stewards of customer data. Slate Auto, the EV startup backed by Jeff Bezos, has made that pitch ahead of the expected launch of its minimalist pickup truck later this year.

“We did a survey of 1,000 consumers, and 91% of them said that data privacy was a key consideration for them. Realistically, it’s not something they engage with every day, but they want to know that they’re, again, in control, and that they have access to the information they need there,” Jones said. “I wouldn’t comment on what our competitors are doing, or anything that’s sort of been in the news there, but certainly it’s something that people don’t trust companies to take care with their data, and we really want to make sure we’re building that trust relationship with them.”

Jones, who joined Ford in 2024 after nearly two decades of working on privacy in the legal, financial, and healthcare fields, said the effort to improve how the automaker communicates with customers about data sharing has been in the works for a while.

“It’s been a journey for, frankly, most of the time I’ve been at Ford,” she said.

Ford’s new website will feature a mix of content that explains what data the company collects, how it uses that information, and how customers can opt in or out.

Opting out of sharing some data will naturally make some modern features inaccessible, Jones said. For example, turning off “connected services” in a Ford vehicle will disable features like real-time navigation and the built-in access to roadside assistance.

But one of the goals of this “privacy promise” push is to better justify why Ford is asking for access to this data and make it clear that the information won’t be used for purposes such as targeted advertising.

Giving Ford access to data about a vehicle’s health, for instance, will provide an owner with better real-time information about whether their car needs maintenance. But it will also “support research and development for future technologies,” Jones said.

“We also do not share information about how our customers are driving their vehicles to data brokers,” Jones said. “I just want to kind of reiterate that we’re not in it to try and monetize data in some way. We’re trying to offer products and services that customers derive value from.”

articles.preview: The North Korean group accused of the world’s largest-ever crypto heist is a state-sponsored collective of elite hackers, groomed from an early age to hunt for “big game.” Artificial intelligence has now provided them with a powerful new tool to swell Kim Jong Un’s coffers and fund his military expansion. Nuclear-armed North Korea maintains a thousands-strong hacker army, but the top unit known as “TraderTraitor,” which the FBI blames for the recent $6.3 billion Binance hack, may only have a dozen or so members, experts say.
articles.body:
The North Korean group accused of the world’s largest-ever crypto heist is a state-sponsored collective of elite hackers, groomed from an early age to hunt for “big game.” Artificial intelligence has now provided them with a powerful new tool to swell Kim Jong Un’s coffers and fund his military expansion.

Nuclear-armed North Korea maintains a thousands-strong hacker army, but the top unit known as “TraderTraitor,” which the FBI blames for the recent $6.3 billion Binance hack, may only have a dozen or so members, experts say.

Unlike garden-variety hackers targeting individual investors, TraderTraitor uses a strategy known as Big Game Hunting, cybersecurity experts say, helped by AI to seek out high-value crypto businesses to compromise. They’ve been so remarkably successful that the revenues they generate could be funding nearly half of North Korea’s banned weapons programs.

articles.title: Digital Agency offers AI app to help draft parliamentary answers
articles.summary: The artificial intelligence app also helps government officials better understand the intent behind lawmakers' questions in advance.
articles.preview: The Digital Agency has started offering, on a trial basis, an app that helps draft answers to lawmakers’ questions in parliament, using its Gennai generative artificial intelligence platform, which is available to about 180,000 government workers. The app also helps government officials better understand the intent behind lawmakers’ questions in advance.
articles.body:
The Digital Agency has started offering, on a trial basis, an app that helps draft answers to lawmakers’ questions in parliament, using its Gennai generative artificial intelligence platform, which is available to about 180,000 government workers.

The app also helps government officials better understand the intent behind lawmakers’ questions in advance.

The agency plans to evaluate the app’s effectiveness during the current session of the Diet, or Japan’s parliament, with the aim to put it into full-scale operation from next year’s ordinary Diet session.

When a lawmaker’s question is entered into the app, AI organizes and analyzes its key points and generates multiple draft answers within minutes based on past government answers and minutes of Diet deliberations.

The app includes a function that adjusts writing styles for different purposes, such as a “policy explanation” mode to clarify policy direction and a “political judgment” mode to reflect political considerations.

Government officials can edit the draft answers directly. The app can also predict follow-up questions from lawmakers. The agency emphasized that officials will remain responsible for clarifying policy decisions, organizing the government’s views and finalizing answers, stressing that decision-making will not be left to AI.

“It’s very good that we can improve our work efficiency and create answers that contribute to deeper Diet deliberations,” digital transformation minister Toshiharu Furukawa told a news conference Friday. “I’d also like to hear feedback from other ministers.”

Data centers are deeply unpopular. But what if we called them something else?

Axios reports that OpenAI is preparing a “PR blitz” for after the midterm elections on Tuesday, as Democrats seem likely to win back the House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, too.

The company’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios that the midterms will be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028,” when he expects AI to be “the issue” in the presidential election.

So OpenAI is to influence the AI debate moving forward, with Lehane discussing several proposals, including the development of AI “speed limits”; finding ways to help people see AI as empowering them in their daily lives; pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards — and yes, rebranding data centers as “AI compute campuses.”

Lehane also described the conversation around data centers (a debate that has pushed Amazon and Microsoft to say they will no longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments) as “good and healthy.”

“Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects,” he said.

articles.body:
The Oct 29 attack is believed to be the largest crypto heist in history and is latest in a string of high-profile cyber thefts linked to Pyongyang.

SEOUL: North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking group has been blamed by US authorities for stealing more than US$6 billion in virtual assets from Binance, in what is believed to be the largest crypto heist in history.

The Oct 29 attack is the latest in a string of high-profile cyber thefts linked to Pyongyang, which has built a formidable hacking operation, generating funds believed to help finance its weapons programme.

Here are five things to know about the group and its place in North Korea’s cyber warfare programme:

WHO ARE THEY?

TraderTraitor is the name given to a North Korean hacking operation linked to the broader Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it hacked Sony Pictures in retaliation for The Interview, a satirical film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Pyongyang has invested heavily in developing its cyber capabilities since at least the mid-1990s, building a formidable force that South Korean intelligence estimated in 2024 comprised around 8,400 personnel.

“North Korea has built a capable cyber force, funnelling many of the country’s top students into computer science and IT training,” the FBI said on its website.

Much of the hacking activity is known to have been directed by Pyongyang’s Reconnaissance General Bureau, its primary foreign intelligence agency.

“The top two students in my class were recruited to the hacking unit,” South Korean MP Park Choong-kwon, who studied at the North’s elite National Defense University before his defection, told AFP in a 2024 interview.

HOW DO THEY OPERATE?

TraderTraitor actors have been known to pose as recruiters offering lucrative jobs to trick victims into downloading malicious software.

The malware can allow hackers to infiltrate victims’ computer systems and steal sensitive information and digital assets.

In a 2024 heist involving the theft of US$308 million from Japanese cryptocurrency exchange DMM Bitcoin, a North Korean hacker posing as a recruiter on LinkedIn contacted an employee of a separate virtual currency wallet software company.

They sent the employee what appeared to be a pre-employment test, which actually contained a malicious line of code.

That allowed the hacker to compromise their system and impersonate the employee, the FBI said.

WHAT HAVE NORTH KOREAN HACKERS DONE?

High-profile cyberattacks attributed to North Korean hackers include the theft of US$81 million from Bangladesh’s central bank in 2016 and the WannaCry ransomware attack that disrupted computers worldwide in 2017.

In 2022, US authorities blamed Lazarus-linked hackers for stealing around US$620 million from the Ronin blockchain network.

The FBI subsequently attributed three more cryptocurrency heists in 2023 to TraderTraitor actors, involving the theft of nearly US$200 million from Atomic Wallet, Alphapo and CoinsPaid.

The scale of the thefts increased dramatically in February 2025, when the FBI blamed TraderTraitor for stealing around US$1.5 billion in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit.

“TraderTraitor actors are proceeding rapidly and have converted some of the stolen assets,” the FBI said at the time.

HOW DOES NORTH KOREA USE STOLEN FUNDS?

The North Korean regime launders stolen cryptocurrency and converts it into cash “through mixing services or private exchanges”, Lim Eul-chul, a professor at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, told AFP.

“The proceeds are then channelled directly into military research, the illicit procurement of weapons components and the defence industry,” he added.

A 2024 United Nations report said proceeds from North Korean cyberattacks “reportedly helped to fund the country’s development of weapons of mass destruction”.

WHY CYBERCRIME?

Analysts say Pyongyang’s illicit cyber activity is driven by its ability to obtain vast sums of money quickly and at “minimal cost”.

“While international sanctions severely restrict North Korea’s ability to earn foreign currency through conventional trade, cyber theft allows it to acquire billions of dollars with minimal personnel and resources,” said Lim of Kyungnam University.

“Hacking offers Pyongyang a way to obtain funds outside conventional banking channels, taking advantage of the pseudonymous and borderless nature of digital assets to bypass financial restrictions,” he added.

Australia’s economy is set for a “sharper, longer slowdown”, major bank economists say, as the Reserve Bank is forced to keep interest rates higher to rid the nation of persistent inflationary pressures.

The RBA is widely expected to hit mortgage holders with a fifth rate hike on Tuesday, in a move that will push the cash rate to its highest since 2008 amid rising worries the economy could even be tipped into recession.

Belinda Allen, the head of Australian economics at CBA, said the extended Middle East conflict, collapsing house prices and a more aggressive central bank would drive real GDP down to just 1% by the middle of next year, nearly half the previous estimate of 1.8%.

Growth through 2027 would be barely stronger at an estimated 1.1%, according to the updated projections.

Allen said she had expected to see “signs of economic recovery” by the New Year, but now sees the economy “bottoming deeper and later”.

This more pessimistic outlook was “mainly given oil has been a lot higher than we had been expecting,” she said.

“Most people thought we would see a resolution to the Middle East conflict by now and oil [prices] looking more normal. Alas, that has not been the case.”

Instead, Brent crude, the global oil price benchmark, has surged from about $US72 a barrel in early July, to back above $US110 in recent days as the conflict broadens and hopes for a peace deal in the near future have all but disappeared.

After Jim Chalmers last month warned the December mid-year budget update would show a more pessimistic economic outlook, analysts at NAB also revealed a major downgrade to their forecasts.

Gareth Spence, the bank’s head of Australian economics, said “unemployment might need to rise higher than we thought” in order to get inflation back under control – a view he said reflected recent comments by top RBA officials.

The economy would grow below trend over 2027 and 2028, Spence said, echoing the forecast of just 1% growth next year.

Spence forecast the key jobless measure would need to rise from 4.7% to as high as 5.4% by the end of next year, as the RBA doubles down on its battle to regain control of inflation.

The CBA forecast was more optimistic, seeing unemployment peak at 5.1% over the same timeframe.

Either way, the RBA’s multi-year strategy of bringing inflation to heel without sacrificing post-Covid employment gains now looks unlikely to be achieved.

As union leaders protested against the anticipated rate hike in front of the RBA’s offices in Sydney on Monday morning, Spence said the risk was that the central bank would have to hike again.

The deteriorating economic outlook comes as new data showed Australia’s property slump remained on track to be one of the deepest on record.

Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, said home prices could fall by as much as 15% before levelling off late next year, with Sydney property values already down by 10% from their recent peak.

Drawing from RBA research, Oliver said a property correction of that magnitude could deliver a substantial hit to the economy, as worried homeowners pull back on spending – a phenomenon known as the “wealth effect”.

A weakening property market will also weigh on homebuilding, Oliver said, adding to the multiplying pressures on the economy.

While an economic contraction was not his “base case”, he warned there was a “significant and rising” risk of recession, the chance of which would rise to as high as 45% should the RBA hike as expected on Tuesday.

“We don’t know the tipping point.”

articles.body:
The workers’ demands reflect mounting pressure from rising living costs and persistent inflation.

DHAKA: Bangladesh's garment factories reopened on Monday (Nov 2) after widespread closures and production disruptions a day earlier, but manufacturers remain concerned about further unrest over workers' demands for higher wages.

The ready-made garment sector accounts for more than 80 per cent of Bangladesh's export earnings, employs about four million workers and contributes around 10 per cent to the gross domestic product (GDP).

The latest unrest disrupted operations in key manufacturing hubs and raised concerns over export shipments and buyer confidence in Bangladesh, the world's second-largest apparel exporter after China, as workers demanded a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka (US$240), up from 12,500 taka.

The demand reflects mounting pressure from rising living costs and persistent inflation. The government formed a six-member minimum wage board on Sunday to review the demand but the move failed to immediately quell unrest.

Workers set up road blockades in several industrial areas on Sunday, with police in the capital Dhaka using tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters.

"Bangladesh has among the lowest garment wages in the world," said Babul Akhter, general secretary of the Bangladesh Garment and Industrial Workers Federation and a workers' representative on the wage board.

"If factory owners cannot pay workers properly, they should negotiate better prices with international buyers. They cannot build a business on the backs of underpaid workers."

“NO WORK, NO PAY PROVISION”

Factory owners said the industry faces higher costs, energy market uncertainty linked to conflict in the Middle East and slowing demand in key export markets.

The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) said demonstrations in multiple cities disrupted operations at 529 factories and affected nearly one million workers.

"The government has already taken a step by forming the wage board. We expect workers to allow the review process to proceed," said BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan.

"If protests break out later in the day and we are forced to shut factories, we will have no option but to invoke the 'no work, no pay' provision," he said, adding industry representatives were scheduled to meet the home minister to discuss the unrest.

Selim Raihan, an economics professor at the University of Dhaka, said workers' demands were understandable given high inflation and suppressed wages could cause further unrest.

However, he cautioned that a substantial wage increase could raise production costs, squeeze exporters' profit margins and weaken Bangladesh's price competitiveness.

"A phased wage adjustment, improved productivity and fairer pricing from international buyers are essential to balancing workers’ welfare with industrial sustainability."
